Q: Kattis 'Digits' question: Why does my first set of code exceed time limit, but my second set does not? A:

For me, code A gives a ValueError rather than TLE upon submission to Kattis.

The input size can be up to a million digits, so it's worth running that through int():

Python 3.10.12 (main, Jan  8 2026, 06:52:19) [GCC 11.4.0] on linux
>>> x = "1" * 1_000_000
>>> int(x)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: Exceeds the limit (4300) for integer string conversion: value has 1000000 digits; use sys.set_int_max_str_digits() to increase the limit

A TLE could occur on other versions of Python, which may have a different value of set_int_max_str_digits(), which ostensibly exists to avoid performance issues.

Now, the accepted code B isolates single-digit numbers (numbers less than 10) and only calls int() on those, avoiding the above performance impact (or error). The check is for an edge case in the recurrence that isn't covered by your recurrence_index implementation: x = 1, which is the final base case of the recurrence for all inputs, the only number for which len(digits) == digits. All other values of x will have at least one step.

Minimizing and refining the working solution makes it easier to see the special handling for "1", letting the main algorithm handle all other inputs:

def recurrence_index(x):
    if x == "1":
        return 1

    iterations = 1

    while True:
        x1 = len(str(x))

        if x1 == x:
            return iterations

        iterations += 1
        x = x1


while True:
    x = input()

    if x == "END":
        break

    print(recurrence_index(x))

In general, for problems like this, it's useful to run the recurrence on a series of input values from, say, 0...1000 and look for trends. Running on just the first 15 numbers shows the anomaly for x = 1 and can be further instrumented to see that 1 is always the final value after a few iterations, at least for small test cases:

for x in range(15):
    print(f"x: {x} -> {recurrence_index(x)} iterations")

Output:

x: 0 -> 2 iterations
x: 1 -> 1 iterations
x: 2 -> 2 iterations
x: 3 -> 2 iterations
x: 4 -> 2 iterations
x: 5 -> 2 iterations
x: 6 -> 2 iterations
x: 7 -> 2 iterations
x: 8 -> 2 iterations
x: 9 -> 2 iterations
x: 10 -> 3 iterations
x: 11 -> 3 iterations
x: 12 -> 3 iterations
x: 13 -> 3 iterations
x: 14 -> 3 iterations

It's worth noticing that, other than 1, the values don't matter, only the number of digits, so you can run tests for larger numbers of digits:

for digits in range(1, 15):
    print(f"digits: {digits} -> {recurrence_index('1' * digits)}")

Output:

digits: 1 -> 1
digits: 2 -> 3
digits: 3 -> 3
digits: 4 -> 3
digits: 5 -> 3
digits: 6 -> 3
digits: 7 -> 3
digits: 8 -> 3
digits: 9 -> 3
digits: 10 -> 4
digits: 11 -> 4
digits: 12 -> 4
digits: 13 -> 4
digits: 14 -> 4

Of course, in this output, the single-digit distinction between 1 and all other numbers less than 10 is lost, but the overall trend shows convergence will occur on larger numbers in just a few iterations.

Furthermore, print(recurrence_index("1" * 1_000_000)) # => 4.

Caching or hardcoding could be used to improve the performance a bit further on non-single digit numbers, since all values of non-one lengths will share the same number of iterations.

Q: Update query in postgreSQL A:

How can we copy data from one column to another in PostgreSQL for very large tables (more than 2 crore / 200 million records per table), where a new column nuid needs to be populated from an existing column noid, across approximately 1000 tables?

Some of these tables have dependencies such as:

Views

Functions

Stored procedures

Indexes

Partitioned tables

We need a safe, enterprise-grade solution that:

Avoids long table locks

Minimizes performance impact

Handles dependent objects correctly

Works reliably at very large scale

Includes complete technical details and SQL code

What is the best approach in PostgreSQL to implement this with minimal risk?

Q: Electron won't read application name A:

I suppose you are using electron-prebuild and because it's a prebuild app (located on your /node_modules/electron-prebuild/dist/Electron.app) has its own name (Electron).

To change the app name you have to rebuild/package your app and it will use the "name" or "productName" from your package.json.

To package your app you can use electron-packager here: https://github.com/electron-userland/electron-packager
